repos.name: Zeatend
repos.description: Turn one Linux server into a Kubernetes cluster that's ready to use, with K3s, RKE2 or KubeSolo.

notes.audience: Developers, DevOps engineers, and self-hosters looking for a lightweight, Kubernetes-native open-source PaaS alternative to Coolify to deploy apps on their VPS.
notes.angle: Zeabur OSS mang trải nghiệm PaaS stateless siêu mượt viết bằng Rust lên cụm Kubernetes mà không cần database riêng, nhưng trên VPS trắng chưa thể cài 1 lệnh như Coolify.

facts.fact: Zeabur OSS là nền tảng PaaS tự host viết bằng Rust, chạy trên Kubernetes và phân phối theo giấy phép Apache-2.0.
Zeabur hoàn toàn không lưu trữ state riêng, không cần database và không tạo custom resources trong cụm Kubernetes.
facts.quote: keeps no state of its own: no database, no custom resources.

facts.fact: Zeatend là công cụ cấu hình máy chủ Linux thành cụm K3s, RKE2 hoặc KubeSolo theo tiêu chuẩn bảo mật CIS benchmark.
facts.quote: It reads one configuration file, /etc/zeatend/config.yaml by default, and installs K3s, RKE2 or KubeSolo hardened to the CIS benchmark

facts.fact: Để tự host Zeabur trên cụm có sẵn, yêu cầu tối thiểu là Kubernetes 1.30 trở lên.
Quá trình cài đặt Zeabur vào cụm yêu cầu quyền admin kubeconfig, kubectl, Helm 4 và công cụ zeabur-identityctl.
facts.quote: A kubeconfig with admin rights for the target cluster, plus kubectl, Helm 4, and zeabur-identityctl.

facts.fact: Hệ thống đăng nhập quản trị Zeabur sử dụng Zeabur Identity qua giao thức HTTPS và hỗ trợ passkey.
facts.quote: Set up a Zeabur Identity client and use Helm to install the management interface with passkey sign-in.

facts.fact: Helm chart chính thức của Zeabur được lưu trữ trên OCI registry của GitHub Container Registry.
facts.quote: The chart is published at oci://ghcr.io/zeabur-oss/charts/zeabur

facts.fact: Người dùng có thể mở dashboard Zeabur trên máy cá nhân mà không cần cài server Zeabur vào cụm thông qua lệnh zeaburctl ui.
facts.quote: If you have a kubeconfig that can connect to the cluster, run zeaburctl ui to open Zeabur locally.

facts.fact: Lệnh zeaburctl ui chỉ lắng nghe trên cổng 127.0.0.1 và tạo token xác thực sử dụng một lần.
facts.quote: zeaburctl ui listens only on 127.0.0.1, on a port assigned by the operating system. The link printed in the terminal includes a one-time token.

facts.fact: Giới hạn kích thước tải mã nguồn từ thư mục qua zeaburctl up là tối đa 256 MiB nén và 1 GiB khi giải nén.
facts.quote: The limits are 256 MiB compressed and 1 GiB extracted.

facts.fact: Phương thức build mặc định của Zeabur khi tạo service mới là railpack, hoặc chỉ định dockerfile.
facts.quote: The default build method is railpack; use --method dockerfile to use a Dockerfile instead.

facts.fact: Phiên đăng nhập quản trị của Zeabur lưu trên bộ nhớ RAM; nâng cấp hoặc thay thế replica pod sẽ yêu cầu đăng nhập lại.
facts.quote: The chart runs one Zeabur replica, and sessions live in memory. Replacing the replica requires signing in again.

facts.fact: Khi gỡ bỏ bảng điều khiển Zeabur bằng Helm, các ứng dụng, ingress, TLS certificate và storage đã triển khai vẫn được giữ nguyên.
facts.quote: Applications and the components that provide ingress, certificates, and storage stay in place.

facts.fact: Gói cài đặt cơ bản của Zeabur theo lộ trình Issue #430 chỉ bao gồm Zeabur, Identity, Traefik, cert-manager và metrics-server.
facts.quote: The first install adds only Zeabur, Identity, Traefik, cert-manager and metrics-server, and skips whatever the cluster already has.

facts.fact: Khác với Zeabur, đối thủ Coolify được viết bằng PHP và cài đặt đơn giản trên VPS thuần thông qua một lệnh cURL script duy nhất.
Coolify hỗ trợ sẵn hơn 360 dịch vụ cài đặt 1 chạm và cơ sở dữ liệu như Postgres, MongoDB, Redis.
facts.quote: Deploy Postgres, MongoDB, Redis & more, plus 360+ one-click services

facts.fact: Một đối thủ PaaS mã nguồn mở khác là Dokploy hỗ trợ cài bằng một lệnh bash và sở hữu hơn 600 template có sẵn.

caveats: Zeabur OSS chưa thể cài trực tiếp bằng 1 lệnh trên bare Linux VPS thông thường như Coolify hay Dokploy mà bắt buộc phải có sẵn cụm Kubernetes (hoặc chờ hoàn thiện dự án Zeatend).
Yêu cầu tối thiểu cụm Kubernetes 1.30 trở lên, Helm 4, Ingress controller (như Traefik) và dịch vụ Zeabur Identity độc lập với chứng chỉ TLS hợp lệ.
Bảng điều khiển Zeabur chỉ chạy 1 replica và lưu session trong RAM, nên mỗi lần restart hoặc upgrade pod thì toàn bộ user đều bị đăng xuất.
Giới hạn upload mã nguồn thư mục trực tiếp bằng zeaburctl up là tối đa 256 MiB nén và 1 GiB sau giải nén.
Việc build app từ thư mục mã nguồn yêu cầu cụm phải cài Zeabur Builder; nếu cài bản personal không có Builder thì chỉ deploy được container image có sẵn.
gaps: Khi nào Zeatend chính thức ra mắt tính năng cài đặt 1 lệnh trọn gói Kubernetes kèm Zeabur trên VPS Linux trắng?
Mức chiếm dụng RAM và CPU tối thiểu của Zeabur OSS (kèm Traefik, Zeabur Identity, cert-manager) trên VPS cấu hình thấp (1GB - 2GB RAM) là bao nhiêu so với Coolify?
Khả năng quản trị sao lưu (database backup) tự động trên Zeabur OSS có sẵn qua giao diện web trực quan như Coolify hay không?

## zeabur-oss/zeabur (https://github.com/zeabur-oss/zeabur)
Description: Deploy apps on your own server from Git, Docker Compose or an app template. Runs on Kubernetes.
Homepage: https://oss.zeabur.com/zeabur
Language: Rust; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-10-24; last push 2026-11-18
Latest release: v0.2.0 (2026-11-08)
README (start):
# Zeabur

**Simple, secure deployments on your own Kubernetes.**

Zeabur is an open-source platform you host yourself. It runs in your cluster (or on your
machine), shows the cluster as projects and services, explains what is wrong in plain words, and lets you
change things safely. It works with the objects you already have, never acts with more rights
than you have, and keeps no state of its own: no database, no custom resources.

**[oss.zeabur.com/zeabur](https://oss.zeabur.com/zeabur/)** shows what Zeabur does, and
**[the documentation](https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/)** covers installing, deploying,
configuring and operating the cluster, and leaving Zeabur, in English,
[繁體中文](https://oss.zeabur.com/zh-TW/docs/zeabur/) and [简体中文](https://oss.zeabur.com/zh-CN/docs/zeabur/).

What needs you, across every project, grouped by where each problem comes from.
One page per project: a map or a list, with what needs attention and what happened.

Diagnoses in plain words, with what to do and the evidence.
Rollouts, usage and domains: progress, CPU and memory against the limits, and whether each domain answers.

Databases with their connection details and a warning when nothing would take over.
The cluster: Kubernetes support dates, node pressure, backups, notifications and components.

Screenshots of the built-in demo data (`cargo run -p zeabur-api --example demo`), taken by `scripts/docs-shots.sh readme`.

## Get started

- **An existing Kubernetes cluster**: install the Helm chart, with sign-in through Zeabur Identity.
  [Install in an existing cluster](https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/install/existing-cluster/)
- **Just you, with your kubeconfig**: `zeaburctl ui` opens Zeabur in your browser on your own
  computer. [zeaburctl](https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/reference/zeaburctl/)
- **A bare Linux server**: not yet. [Zeatend](https://github.com/zeabur-oss/zeatend) will set up
  Kubernetes there, and one command will install Zeabur
  ([#430](https://github.com/zeabur-oss/zeabur/issues/430)).

[Releases](https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/reference/releases/) lists what a release contains
and how to verify it.

## Build from source

In the [Nix](https://nixos.org) dev shell, which provides every tool:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/zeabur-oss/zeabur && cd zeabur
nix develop
./scripts/build-ui.sh
ZEABUR_UI_DIST="$PWD/web/dist" cargo build --release --locked -p zeaburctl
./target/release/zeaburctl ui                  # --context  for another context
```

`zeaburctl ui` listens on a random loopback port, opens the browser, and makes every request
with your current kubeconfig context.

## Contributing

- [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md): environment, checks, dependency policy, tests.
- [Developer docs](docs/internal/): crates, testing, wording, releasing.
- [`docs/`](docs/) holds the sources of the documentation; edit a page there and it is published
  to [oss.zeabur.com](https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/).

## License and credits

Apache-2.0. Contributions are accepted under the [Developer Certificate of Origin](DCO).

Third-party content in this repository:

- [Zeabur Catalog](https://github.com/zeabur-oss/catalog), embedded from its release bundle at the
  commit in `flake.lock` (Apache-2.0).
- Kubernetes' release schedule in `crates/zeabur-catalog/src/versions.rs`, from
  [kubernetes/website](https://github.com/kubernetes/website) `data/releases` (CC BY 4.0, The
  Kubernetes Authors).
- Rendered manifests of upstream Helm charts in `fixtures/charts`, test input only, each under
  its chart's license (Apache-2.0 or MIT; listed in `fixtures/charts/README.md`).

The web interface is built with [@zeabur-oss/design-system](https://github.com/zeabur-oss/design-system)
(Apache-2.0), which contains shadcn/ui's components, theme and base styles (MIT), the Inter and
JetBrains Mono fonts (SIL Open Font License 1.1) and the Zeabur logo; its README lists their
notices. The built interface, embedded in the binary and the image, includes those fonts and
the logo.

The container image includes Mozilla's CA certificate bundle as packaged by nixpkgs (MPL-2.0).

## coollabsio/coolify (https://github.com/coollabsio/coolify)
Description: An open-source, self-hostable PaaS alternative to Vercel, Heroku & Netlify that lets you easily deploy static sites, databases, full-stack applications and 360+ one-click services on your own servers.

[](https://github.com/coollabsio/coolify/releases)  [](https://coollabs.io/discord) [](https://github.com/coollabsio/coolify/commits)

## What is Coolify?

Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable platform for deploying **any application, database, or service** on your own servers. It is an alternative to Heroku, Netlify, and Vercel.

It gives you the experience of a managed cloud platform while running on infrastructure you control. This could be a VPS, a bare-metal server, a Raspberry Pi, or even an old laptop running Linux. You only need an SSH connection.

Your configurations stay on your servers. If you stop using Coolify, your running resources continue to work and remain manageable.

Coolify is fully free and open source, as described in our [philosophy](https://coolify.io/philosophy), with an optional managed service, [Coolify Cloud](https://app.coolify.io). **Nothing is locked behind a paywall.**

## Key features

| Area | Highlights |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Deploy** | Any stack from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea or a Docker image, via Railpack, Dockerfile or Compose, with auto-deploy, PR previews, webhooks, rolling updates & rollbacks |
| **Databases & services** | Deploy Postgres, MongoDB, Redis & more, plus 360+ one-click services |
| **Networking** | Reverse proxy with automatic HTTPS, custom domains & isolated Docker networks |
| **Servers** | Manage unlimited servers over SSH, or provision new ones from hosting providers |
| **Monitor** | Real-time metrics, logs, web terminal & health checks |
| **Operations** | Scheduled backups & tasks, environment variables & secrets, notifications |
| **Teams & integrations** | Teams with access control, plus a REST API, CLI & MCP server |

This is just a highlight — there's much more.

## Get started

Install Coolify on a supported server with one command:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://cdn.coollabs.io/coolify/install.sh | bash
```

Read the [installation guide](https://coolify.io/docs/start-with-self-hosted) for requirements. You can also review the [installation script](./scripts/install.sh) before you run it.

## Install Zeabur in an existing cluster | Zeabur OSS
URL: https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/install/existing-cluster/
Description: Set up a Zeabur Identity client and use Helm to install the management interface with passkey sign-in.

Skip to content
Open Source
Menu
On this page
Overview
Install Zeabur in an existing cluster

Set up a Zeabur Identity client and use Helm to install the management interface with passkey sign-in.

Register a Zeabur client in Zeabur Identity, store the client secret in the cluster, and install the Helm chart. Then open Zeabur, sign in with a passkey, and view existing namespaces.

Prepare sign-in and HTTPS
Section titled “Prepare sign-in and HTTPS”
A kubeconfig with admin rights for the target cluster, plus kubectl, Helm 4, and zeabur-identityctl.
Kubernetes 1.30 or later. By default, the chart creates project member roles and uses ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to limit which Namespace fields Developers can change. This API is generally available starting in 1.30.
Zeabur Identity with sign-in available over HTTPS, and a kube-apiserver that trusts the Kubernetes tokens it issues. See Zeabur Identity's get started guide for installation instructions.
An HTTPS domain for Zeabur, a working Ingress controller, and a TLS secret for that domain. The examples use Traefik, zeabur.example.com, and zeabur-tls.
The Zeabur version to install. The chart is published at oci://ghcr.io/zeabur-oss/charts/zeabur, and its default image is pinned to the digest for the same version. See Release artifacts for download and verification instructions. The examples use <version> for the version number.

Zeabur's sign-in domain and the public domains for services you deploy later are configured separately. Get sign-in working for the management interface first, then prepare DNS and certificates for applications.

Register the Zeabur client
Section titled “Register the Zeabur client”

The example uses https://identity.example.com as the Identity issuer. Replace both domains with their actual values, and run this command with the cluster admin's kubeconfig:

zeabur-identityctl client create zeabur \
  --type confidential \
  --audience kubernetes \
  --display-name Zeabur \
  --redirect-uri https://zeabur.example.com/auth/callback \
  --home-url https://zeabur.example.com/ \
  | kubectl apply -f -

The command prints the client secret once, on stderr. Create the namespace, then read the value interactively in Bash rather than passing it as a command argument:

kubectl create namespace zeabur
read -rs CLIENT_SECRET
printf %s "$CLIENT_SECRET" | kubectl -n zeabur create secret generic zeabur-oidc \
  --from-file=client-secret=/dev/stdin
unset CLIENT_SECRET

After running read, paste the client secret and press Enter. Keeping the value out of command arguments prevents other users on the machine from seeing it in the process list. The chart records only the secret's name, so the value stays out of Helm's release records.

Install the management interface
Section titled “Install the management interface”

Make sure zeabur-tls is in the zeabur namespace, then run:

helm install zeabur oci://ghcr.io/zeabur-oss/charts/zeabur \
  --version <version> \
  --namespace zeabur \
  --set clusterName=production \
  --set publicUrl=https://zeabur.example.com \
  --set issuer.url=https://identity.example.com \
  --set issuer.clientSecret.existingSecret=zeabur-oidc \
  --set ingress.enabled=true \
  --set ingress.className=traefik \
  --set ingress.tls.secretName=zeabur-tls
kubectl -n zeabur rollout status deployment/zeabur

clusterName is the cluster name shown in the interface. The domain in publicUrl must match the client's callback domain. The chart refuses public URLs that use HTTP or include a path.

This installation adds Zeabur's Deployment, Service, Ingress, configuration, and plan key, along with the ClusterRoles and Namespace admission policy for project members. The chart doesn't bind the member roles to anyone. After signing in, an admin sets each person's access on the Members page.

Admins who sign in with an admin account have full cluster rights, with no additional setup in Zeabur. See Permissions for admin accounts, session limits, and the sign-in settings on the Settings page.

Sign in and check existing services
Section titled “Sign in and check existing services”

Open https://zeabur.example.com and sign in with a passkey. Go to Projects, find an existing application under Other namespaces, and open it to view its services.

To keep it listed as a project, select Use this namespace, then review and apply the change. This only adds a project label. It doesn't move the Deployments, Services, or data inside.

If you can sign in but can't see services, check the user's Kubernetes rights first. Zeabur reads the cluster with the signed-in person's token. Zeabur's own ServiceAccount can only use kubectl terminal replicas in zeabur-terminals. An admin can grant project roles on the Members page.

Give new services a public URL
Section titled “Give new services a public URL”

Prepare an application domain, such as apps.example.com. Point the DNS record for *.apps.example.com at the Ingress controller's address, and prepare a cert-manager ClusterIssuer that can issue certificates, such as letsencrypt. Update the same release:

helm upgrade zeabur oci://ghcr.io/zeabur-oss/charts/zeabur \
  --version <version> \
  --namespace zeabur --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set 'domains.suffixes={apps.example.com}' \
  --set domains.clusterIssuer=letsencrypt

With --reset-then-reuse-values, Helm starts from the new chart's defaults, including the image, then applies the values you set. With --reuse-values, Helm also keeps the old chart's defaults, and the image stays on the old version.

When you deploy web in the shop project, the form suggests web-shop.apps.example.com. You can list multiple application domains separated by commas; the first is the default. You can also change them later in the Domains section of the Cluster page, which checks DNS records and lists the records to add. See Set up DNS records. If domains.suffixes is empty, enter the full domain by hand. If domains.clusterIssuer is empty, new services' public URLs use HTTP.

These settings only name the issuer services should use. Prepare the ClusterIssuer and DNS first; Zeabur doesn't create them from these two values.

Trust a private CA
Section titled “Trust a private CA”

If Zeabur Identity, a registry, object storage, or GitHub Enterprise uses a certificate signed by a private CA, or the cluster connects through a proxy that inspects TLS, put the CA certificates in a ConfigMap in Zeabur's namespace and set extraTrustedCA.configMap:

kubectl -n zeabur create configmap corp-ca --from-file=ca.crt=corp-ca.pem
helm upgrade zeabur oci://ghcr.io/zeabur-oss/charts/zeabur \
  --version <version> \
  --namespace zeabur --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set extraTrustedCA.configMap=corp-ca

If the certificates are in a secret, set extraTrustedCA.secret instead. Use only one of these settings. The key is ca.crt by default; change it with extraTrustedCA.key. The file may hold several certificates.

Zeabur trusts these certificates in addition to the built-in Mozilla CA bundle when signing in to Identity, reading images, reading backups from object storage, and connecting to GitHub. Zeabur reads the file when it starts, so after you change the config file, run kubectl -n zeabur rollout restart deployment/zeabur.

zeabur-installer sets issuer.caBundle and builds.caBundle to reference the local CA that signs Identity's certificate and Zot's CA, respectively. Zeabur trusts them alongside extraTrustedCA, so you don't need to set them yourself.

Common failures
Section titled “Common failures”
Situation	What to check
The browser can't open Zeabur	Check public DNS, the Ingress class, the TLS secret, and connectivity to the entry point. Confirm the Deployment is ready before checking the entry point.
Sign-in doesn't return to Zeabur	Check publicUrl, the /auth/callback registered in Identity, and issuer.url.
Identity uses a private CA	Set extraTrustedCA so Zeabur trusts the CA that signed Identity's certificate. See Trust a private CA.
Read requests are denied after sign-in	Check the member's identity and groups in Identity, then check the target namespace's RoleBinding. See Permissions reference.
A new service is ready, but its URL doesn't work	Check the application domain's DNS and certificate. The management interface and applications use different domains, which need separate configuration.
You need to sign in again after an upgrade	The chart runs one Zeabur replica, and sessions live in memory. Replacing the replica requires signing in again.
Manage the chart with GitOps
Section titled “Manage the chart with GitOps”

Zeabur uses a key to sign reviewed changes. The chart creates that key on the first install and reads it back on subsequent helm upgrade runs. Argo CD and helm template generate manifests without connecting to the cluster, so they generate a new key each time, and the new key invalidates changes you reviewed but haven't applied yet. For these tools, create a fixed key first, then set planKey.existingSecret:

kubectl -n zeabur create secret generic zeabur-plan-key \
  --from-literal=plan-key="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"

Set planKey.existingSecret to zeabur-plan-key. To view all chart settings, run helm show values oci://ghcr.io/zeabur-oss/charts/zeabur --version <version>.

Install the components Zeabur needs
Section titled “Install the components Zeabur needs”

If the cluster wasn't installed with zeabur-installer, Zeabur's components page only shows status; it doesn't install components. Use zeaburctl components export to print a component's manifests, then apply them with kubectl or commit them to a GitOps repository:

zeaburctl components export certificates/cert-manager --format flux > cert-manager.yaml

For K3s or RKE2 clusters, use the default helmchart format so the built-in helm-controller handles installation. For other clusters, use helm, flux, or argocd.

Remove the management interface
Section titled “Remove the management interface”
helm uninstall zeabur --namespace zeabur

Applications and the components that provide ingress, certificates, and storage stay in place. The member roles the chart created are removed with the release, so give members their rights another way. See Remove Zeabur for the full list of what stays and the steps to migrate sign-in.

## zeaburctl | Zeabur OSS
URL: https://oss.zeabur.com/docs/zeabur/reference/zeaburctl/
Description: Open Zeabur with the current kubeconfig, upload a folder, check a cluster, or export component installation manifests and commands.

Skip to content
Open Source
Menu
On this page
Overview
zeaburctl

Open Zeabur with the current kubeconfig, upload a folder, check a cluster, or export component installation manifests and commands.

If you have a kubeconfig that can connect to the cluster, run zeaburctl ui to open Zeabur locally. Reads, Review changes, and confirmed changes all use that context's permissions. You don't need to install a Zeabur server in the cluster first.

Download the binary for your operating system and processor from Releases and verification. When a newer version is out, zeaburctl prints one line about it, at most once a day. See Update check for what it sends and how to turn it off.

Commands
Section titled “Commands”
zeaburctl --version
zeaburctl ui
zeaburctl ui --context production --no-browser
zeaburctl doctor --context production --output json
zeaburctl up ./site --project shop --service site
zeaburctl components export certificates/cert-manager

ui, doctor, and up each accept --context. If omitted, they use the current context in kubeconfig. The commands don't modify kubeconfig.

Command	Result	What it changes
ui	Opens Zeabur in a local browser	Installs no components in the cluster. Changes applied in the interface go directly to the cluster
doctor	Checks the cluster version, components, and Zeabur Identity settings	Reads only; doesn't change settings
up	Uploads a folder to a service created from a folder and starts a build	Updates the service's Build and pushes the folder to the registry
components export	Prints manifests or Helm commands to install Catalog components	Doesn't connect to the cluster or change anything
ui
Section titled “ui”
Option	Default and purpose
--context <name>	The current context in kubeconfig
--no-browser	Doesn't open a browser automatically; still prints the link
--metrics-service <namespace/name:port>	Specifies a Kubernetes Service that supports the Prometheus HTTP API. You can also use the ZEABUR_METRICS_SERVICE environment variable

For example, to read usage history from an existing Prometheus installation:

zeaburctl ui --context production \
  --metrics-service monitoring/prometheus:9090

By default, Zeabur reads from the VictoriaMetrics installation in Zeabur Catalog: observability/vmsingle-vm-victoria-metrics-k8s-stack:8428. Zeabur reads through the Kubernetes API's Service proxy, so you also need get services/proxy permission for this Service. Live CPU and memory usage comes from metrics-server.

zeaburctl ui listens only on 127.0.0.1, on a port assigned by the operating system. The link printed in the terminal includes a one-time token. Opening it for the first time exchanges the token for a browser session. The same link won't work again.

Press Ctrl-C to close the local interface. Applied changes stay in the cluster; unapplied drafts aren't written to it. When you run zeaburctl ui again, open the newly printed link.

doctor
Section titled “doctor”
zeaburctl doctor
zeaburctl doctor --context production --output json
Option	Values
--context <name>	Specifies a kubeconfig context
--output <format>	text (default) or json

The JSON output has a top-level checks array. Each item has name, status, findings, and fix fields. status is ok, warning, critical, skipped, or error. If the command can't read something, it lists the missing permissions.

Exit code	Meaning
0	No issues need attention; some checks may be skipped
1	There are warnings
2	There are critical issues, or the command arguments are incorrect
3	The command can't connect to the cluster, or checks can't run

When results differ, critical issues take precedence over warnings, which take precedence over checks that couldn't run. skipped doesn't affect the exit code. Monitoring tools need to read checks separately to find out which checks were skipped.

On a cluster without the Zeabur dashboard, zeaburctl doctor skips the Zeabur Identity checks, because only the dashboard needs Zeabur Identity. A personal installation has no dashboard, and neither does a cluster you only open with zeaburctl ui. doctor looks for a Deployment labeled app.kubernetes.io/name=zeabur in the projects you can see. If it can't read the namespaces or a project's Deployments, it runs the checks anyway.

Whether kube-apiserver trusts the Zeabur Identity issuer is defined in the control plane's AuthenticationConfiguration file. RBAC can't read this file, so zeaburctl doctor marks this check as skipped. To check it on the host, use zeabur-installer doctor.

up
Section titled “up”
zeaburctl up [folder] [--project <project>] [--service <service>]

Uploads a folder to the cluster and starts a build. If you omit the folder, the command uses the current folder. If the service doesn't exist, the command creates it. The project must already exist; the command doesn't create projects.

The command reads the Zeabur URL and Zeabur Identity address from the zeabur-info config file in the cluster's kube-public namespace. No separate configuration is needed. Anyone signed in to the cluster can read this config file; unauthenticated users can't. To use a different URL, add --server or set the ZEABUR_SERVER environment variable.

The command uses the same API and change plans as the web interface. You don't need to know the registry address.

Server mode and local mode
Section titled “Server mode and local mode”

When the command starts, it prints a line showing which mode it's using.

Mode	When it's used	How it sends the folder
Server mode	kubeconfig uses a Zeabur Identity token to sign in, and the cluster has zeabur-info	Sends the folder to Zeabur in the cluster, which pushes it to the registry
Local mode	All other cases, such as an admin kubeconfig from the installer, a cloud provider token, a ServiceAccount token, or a cluster without a Zeabur server	Runs the same steps on your computer, like zeaburctl ui, then pushes to the registry from that computer

Local mode connects directly to the Kubernetes API with the credentials in kubeconfig. It doesn't send those credentials anywhere else. With the admin kubeconfig from the installer, you can run up without any additional configuration.

Local mode also requires:

Zeabur Builder installed in the cluster. If it's missing, the command stops before uploading. A personal installation doesn't include Zeabur Builder by default; you need to select it during installation. If it isn't installed, deploy an image instead.
Access to the registry. If the registry is inside the cluster, such as zot.zot.svc:5000, the command automatically forwards a port through the Kubernetes API, like kubectl port-forward. You need get services, list endpointslices, and create pods/portforward permissions in the registry's namespace, plus read access to the CA config file for the registry's certificate. Administrators have these permissions; a project's Developer role doesn't.
zeabur-info in the cluster. The command reads the registry location from it. Without a Zeabur server in the cluster, the command can't create new services and doesn't automatically forward ports.
Sign-in and permissions
Section titled “Sign-in and permissions”

The command signs in with the current context in kubeconfig. Use --context to specify another context. Both modes use your permissions for uploads and changes. They can't do anything you don't have permission to do.

The command sends only tokens issued by Zeabur Identity to Zeabur in the cluster. It doesn't send cloud provider tokens (such as GKE or EKS tokens), ServiceAccount tokens, static tokens, or client certificates to Zeabur; it uses local mode instead. Zeabur also accepts only tokens issued by Zeabur Identity and treats other tokens as unauthenticated.

In server mode, the Zeabur URL must use https://. You can use http:// only when testing on your own computer (localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ::1).

Choose a project and service
Section titled “Choose a project and service”

When running in a terminal, the command prompts you to choose a project from a list if you omit --project. If you omit --service, it asks for a service name, defaulting to the folder name.

If the service doesn't exist, the command asks for confirmation before creating it. Add --yes to skip this confirmation.

In scripts or CI, the command doesn't prompt. You must specify the project and service with --project and --service. If the service doesn't exist, the command creates it without requiring --yes.

A new service has the same contents as one created with Upload a folder in the web interface, including a Build and Deployment. If you pass --port, the command also creates a Kubernetes Service and sets the PORT environment variable. Without a port, the service doesn't accept connections. The default build method is railpack; use --method dockerfile to use a Dockerfile instead.

If the service already exists, the command keeps its build settings. If the service builds from Git, the command rejects the upload without changing anything.

Packaging and uploading
Section titled “Packaging and uploading”

Packaging follows the same rules as web uploads. It skips files excluded by .gitignore and .dockerignore, as well as .git. The limits are 256 MiB compressed and 1 GiB extracted.

The command sends a tar.gz archive. It keeps executable permissions, and symbolic links that point inside the uploaded folder.

The upload has three steps, in order:

Request an upload token from the Build. This is a change plan that the command applies directly.
Push the archive to the registry. In server mode, Zeabur pushes it; in local mode, your computer does.
Write the digest to the Build to start the build. This is also a change plan that the command applies directly.

These are the same change plans the web interface uses. Running the command confirms that you want to apply them; the command doesn't ask again. When creating a new service, the service creation plan already includes the upload token request.

Options
Section titled “Options”
Option	Default and purpose
--server <address>	The URL for server mode. Defaults to the URL in zeabur-info. Specify a different URL, such as https://zeabur.example.com, or use the ZEABUR_SERVER environment variable
--project <project>	The existing project for the service. If omitted in a terminal, prompts you to choose from a list. Required in scripts and CI
--service <service>	The service name. If omitted in a terminal, prompts for a name, defaulting to the folder name. Required in scripts and CI
--context <name>	Defaults to the current context in kubeconfig
--method railpack|dockerfile	The build method for a new service. Defaults to railpack
--port <port>	The port where a new service accepts connections. Configures both the Kubernetes Service and the PORT environment variable. If omitted, the service doesn't accept connections
--yes	Skips confirmation before creating a new service in a terminal
components export
Section titled “components export”
zeaburctl components export <capability>/<id>... [--format helmchart|helm|flux|argocd] [--profile single-node|multi-node]

Prints installation manifests or commands for Catalog components on clusters that weren't installed with zeabur-installer. You can name several components; their output comes one after another. The output comes from zeaburctl's built-in Catalog, with pinned versions and configuration values. The command doesn't connect to the cluster, so it doesn't need --context.

Option	Default and purpose
--format	helmchart: a K3s/RKE2 HelmChart, installed by helm-controller. helm: a helm upgrade --install command. flux: a Flux source and HelmRelease. argocd: an Argo CD Application
--profile	single-node. Use multi-node for the Catalog's multi-node configuration values

Values you need to supply appear as <name> placeholders. Replace them with actual values first. If a component needs host access, the output first sets its namespace to privileged. If K3s or RKE2 includes the same component, the start of the output explains how to disable the built-in ve

Zeabur Zeatend

A Kubernetes cluster manager in the spirit of k3sup. It sets up and manages K3s, RKE2 and KubeSolo clusters on hosts over SSH, with a terminal UI.

Zeatend is made by the Zeabur project and is in early development.

Usage

Today zeatend runs on the Linux host it installs, as root. It reads one configuration file, /etc/zeatend/config.yaml by default, and installs K3s, RKE2 or KubeSolo hardened to the CIS benchmark:

distribution: k3s # k3s (default), rke2 or kubesolo
host:
  tlsSan: [k8s.example.com]

K3s (v1.37.2+k3s1) and RKE2 (v1.37.2+rke2r1) install Kubernetes 1.37. KubeSolo v1.3.0 installs Kubernetes 1.36.6, because KubeSolo has no 1.37 release yet.

zeatend plan shows what apply would install and runs the host checks; --json prints the plan as JSON.
zeatend apply installs, or brings an install in line with the configuration. It is safe to run again.
zeatend uninstall removes K3s, RKE2 or KubeSolo and the files zeatend wrote. It shows what it removes and keeps, and asks first (--yes skips the question). Volumes stay unless you add --delete-volumes.

On a host with systemd, apply runs the install in the transient unit zeatend-install-<id>.service and shows its progress. When the SSH session ends, the install goes on. Run sudo zeatend apply again to follow it: while an install unit runs, apply shows that unit's progress from the journal and starts nothing new. journalctl -u 'zeatend-install-*' has the full output. apply --foreground runs the install in the same process instead, and apply --json prints the progress as JSON lines.

A configuration with a join section joins this host to an existing K3s or RKE2 cluster:

distribution: k3s
join:
  server: https://10.0.0.5:6443 # port 9345 on RKE2
  role: worker # or server, on RKE2 only
  tokenFile: /etc/zeatend/join-token # mode 0600

Revised 2026-11-12
The component engine does not take over the installer's Helm values merge. CRDs come from the catalog CI, which renders them with real Helm (Epic: use upstream mechanisms instead of home-grown ones #439).
The engine uses kube-rs and the shared readiness module (fix(graph): StatefulSet and DaemonSet readiness follows kstatus, shared with the rollout panel #434, Epic: typed reads and shared readiness checks in the installer #428).
Open question

Not decided. The chart runner capability: keep k3s helm-controller, or use Flux's HelmRelease, whose observedGeneration and Ready condition would remove our HelmChart wait? helm-controller stays the decision until this is answered.

This is a tracking issue. It has no implementation pull request of its own.

Goal

What can be done through the cluster API with the person's own rights belongs to Zeabur, first through zeaburctl install and then the Components page. Anything that needs a node shell or does not yet have a cluster belongs to Zeatend. Adding a component is one kind of Component change that starts with five typed reads (ingress, certificates, metrics API, chart runner, default storage class), and each capability resolves to use yours, install ours, or explain what is missing.

Scope
No presets. The first install adds only Zeabur, Identity, Traefik, cert-manager and metrics-server, and skips whatever the cluster already has.
Existing K3s and RKE2 clusters are taken over as they are. EKS and GKE use the desktop app plus zeaburctl install.
VictoriaMetrics is not installed by default. It becomes two one-click components, usage history with notifications and past logs.
The baseline NetworkPolicy stays. On KubeSolo and on network plugins that do not enforce it, the operation warns that it will not take effect.
The minimum Kubernetes is 1.30, clusters managed by Flux use zeaburctl components export, and the whole setup file of all components is replaced by zeaburctl components export --selection.
The old installer is deleted once the new terminal UI in Zeatend has shipped.
Reinstall (installer: reinstall a component that can't be upgraded in place #346): a component that cannot be upgraded in place, or whose release is stuck, is removed and installed again as one confirmed plan that says what it loses.
Blocked by
The plan/apply, installer read, operation and rights epics.
Zeatend publishing the install command before the old installer goes.
